title: Edge stream multiplexing latency investigation - on-call notes
summary: P1 incident: intermittent end-to-end streaming latency spikes originating from edge mux layer during high-fanout requests. Client-observed tail latency increases (95th -> 99.9th) and occasional streaming resets. No customer data loss reported; some sessions required reconnects. Impact window ~2026-03-10 03:40-04:25 UTC for subset of regions behind eu-west-edge cluster.
incident_timeline:
03:38 UTC - Oncall alert: streaming tail-latency alarm (eu-west-edge) triggered (95th up 3x).
03:40 UTC - Paging + SRE Slack incident channel created (#sre-ops).
03:42 UTC - Initial triage: metrics show rise in streaming write latency and queue depth on edge mux nodes; host CPU normal, network TX spikes observed.
03:48 UTC - Temporary mitigation: increase mux worker concurrency cap on affected nodes (hotpatch) -> partial improvement.
03:55 UTC - Observed session resets (stream disconnects) correlated with mux queue flush events; client SDKs retransmitted increasing request-rate.
04:05 UTC - Rollback of recent edge release (edge-mux v1.6.3) suspected; rolled back to v1.6.1 in eu-west-edge cluster -> latency stabilizes after ~7 minutes.
04:20 UTC - Monitoring shows return to baseline; incident channel moved to post-incident notes.
04:25 UTC - Pager closed (ops lead), follow-up actions assigned.
observations:
- Pattern: high fanout streaming requests (many small parallel streams per connection) correlated with mux worker-side queue pressure.
- Mux metrics: per-connection multiplexing table growth, spikes in per-connection write buffer flush latency.
- Autoscaler did not trigger because node-level CPU was within thresholds; issue surfaced in intra-node event loop saturation, not OS CPU.
- Recent code path change in v1.6.3 added a best-effort per-stream ack which increased number of event-loop callbacks under high-fanout.
- Edge telemetry lacked a clear event-loop latency metric (we had only CPU, network, application-level latency).
root_causes:
1) Code change (edge-mux v1.6.3) introduced additional async callbacks per stream that do not yield before scheduling follow-up work. Under high-fanout this caused event-loop starvation and long tail latencies.
2) Monitoring gaps: no direct event-loop latency or per-worker callback-queue length metric; existing alarms were CPU/network only and missed this class of saturation.
3) Autoscaling and circuit-breaker thresholds tuned to node CPU/network, not event-loop saturation metrics, so there was no automatic mitigation.
immediate_mitigations:
- Hotpatch: reduced mux worker concurrency and introduced a small micro-yield between per-stream callbacks to throttle callbacks (rolled into v1.6.3-hotfix).
- Rollback: rolled back eu-west-edge to v1.6.1 where pattern not reproducible.
- Short-term config: lowered per-connection maximum parallel streams for high-risk teams for 24 hours.
- Communication: notified CS and impacted customers via status.redwood.ai (incident update), and posted summary to #customer-impact.
long_term_actions:
- Revert problematic callback pattern permanently and add micro-yield shims in stream handler (runtime PR linked).
- Add event-loop latency and per-worker callback-queue length to edge telemetry (metrics + dashboards).
- Update autoscaler to include event-loop latency-based scaling policy and add a degraded-mode fallback that reduces multiplexing concurrency when event-loop latency > X ms.
- Implement circuit-breaker at proxy layer to stop accepting new streams for a connection when per-connection buffer/flush latency crosses threshold.
- Postmortem write-up + exec summary for leadership (owner: Daniel Cho, due 2026-03-17).
- Create a canary plan for future edge releases focusing on high-fanout streaming workloads (owner: Maya Patel).
runbook_updates:
- New runbook section: 'edge-stream-event-loop-saturation' with playbook steps: identify affected cluster, reduce mux concurrency, rollback edge version, apply per-connection throttle.
- Add checklist item: run high-fanout streaming load test against new edge builds in pre-prod canary before rollouts.
- Add explicit metric thresholds and alarm recipes: event_loop_latency_99 > 200ms -> page SRE and trigger temporary per-connection caps.
- Add runbook note: when rolling back, ensure tracing context retention to correlate reconnects.
- Update runbook ownership: on-call -> eng-sre, release-engineering -> responsible for pre-rollout canary verification.
oncall_notes:
Triage shorthand and lessons: 
- If you see streaming tail latency without CPU/network anomalies, suspect event-loop saturation; check per-worker queue-length and recent edge releases.
- Hotpatching concurrency caps can be done without full deploy (instructions in runbook). Use caution: too low -> client timeouts.
- Rollback is the safest mitigation when a new edge release correlates with pattern. Coordinate with release-engineering to prevent Canary drift.
- Slack channels: use #sre-ops for ops coordination, and tag @release-eng. Use incident template when paging.
Open questions / TODOs: 
- What safe default per-connection parallel streams should we enforce? (proposal: 8 for public clusters)
- How to measure per-connection multiplex pressure at scale without high-cardinality explosion in metrics? Explore sampling + histograms.
- Run a controlled chaos test that simulates client reconnect storms to validate reconnect backoff in SDKs.
Notes to self: keep copy of hotpatch steps in pingable doc, add contact alias for release lead.
